renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: authenticity_plane
  title: Authenticity plane
  description: |-
    Each point is a library: its mean mapped fragment length on the horizontal axis and the C to T frequency at the first 5' base on the vertical axis, with the marker sized by mapped fragments. It answers whether a library carries the two signals of ancient DNA, short fragments and terminal deamination.
    How to read: a library high on the vertical axis and short on the horizontal one combines damage and fragmentation, as expected for ancient DNA. A long, undamaged library looks modern, which may be a contaminant, and a short but undamaged one may be over-sheared modern DNA. No pass mark is drawn because none is defined by the tool, so judge each library against the others and the extraction history.
    Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median C to T frequency at the first 5' base of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of DamageProfiler.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17715061/ and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22479540/
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    reference_line: horizontal
    reference_stat: median
    x_title: Mean fragment length (bp)
    y_title: C to T at the first 5' base
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    x: mean_length
    y: ct_5p_first
    label: sample
    color: sample
    size: n_reads

- component: figure
  title: Terminal deamination per library
  description: |-
    Each bar is a library: the mean of its C to T frequency at the first 5' base and its G to A frequency at the first 3' base. It answers which libraries show the most damage at the read ends.
    How to read: a higher bar means stronger terminal deamination, the signature of ancient DNA. A bar near the background level is a library without clear damage, so check its fragment length too.
    Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median terminal deamination of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of DamageProfiler.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17715061/
  visu_type: bar
  dict_kwargs:
    x: sample
    y: terminal_damage
    color: sample
    labels:
      sample: Library
      terminal_damage: Terminal deamination (mean of 5' C to T and 3' G to A)
  reference_lines:
  - axis: y
    stat: median
    column: terminal_damage

- component: card
  title: C to T at the 5' end
  description: |-
    The hero number is the mean frequency of C to T substitutions at the first 5' base over the libraries, and the box shows the spread. It answers how damaged the libraries are at the 5' end.
    How to read: a higher value means stronger deamination. A library far below its peers has little damage, which is expected for modern or repaired libraries.
    Source: https://damageprofiler.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contents/output.html
  column: ct_5p_first
  aggregation: average
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: mean, with its spread
  headline: true

- component: card
  title: Mean fragment length
  description: |-
    The hero number is the mean mapped fragment length in bases over the libraries, and the box shows the spread. It answers how fragmented the DNA is.
    How to read: shorter fragments fit ancient DNA, which is fragmented by depurination. A library with much longer fragments than its peers may hold modern DNA.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17715061/
  column: mean_length
  aggregation: average
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: mean, with its spread

- component: card
  title: G to A at the 3' end
  description: |-
    The hero number is the mean frequency of G to A substitutions at the first 3' base over the libraries, and the box shows the spread. It answers how damaged the libraries are at the 3' end.
    How to read: on a double-stranded library the 3' G to A signal reflects deamination at the 5' end of the complementary strand, so it should agree with the 5' C to T signal. A strong 5' signal with no 3' signal is not explained by that pattern, so check how the library was built.
    Source: https://damageprofiler.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contents/output.html and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22479540/
  column: ga_3p_first
  aggregation: average
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: mean, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Mapped fragments
  description: |-
    The hero number is the count of mapped fragments over the libraries, and the histogram shows how the libraries spread. It answers how much data backs the damage estimates.
    How to read: estimates from a library with few fragments are noisy, so treat its damage and length values with caution.
  column: n_reads
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: histogram
  caption: distribution across libraries

- component: table
  title: Authenticity table
  description: |-
    Each row is a library with its terminal damage at both ends, its background substitution rate, its fragment length and its mapped fragments. It answers the exact values behind the authenticity tiles.
    How to read: sort by terminal damage to rank libraries, then compare with the fragment length.

- component: advanced_viz
  id: fragment_length_profile
  title: Fragment length distribution
  description: |-
    Each line is a library and strand: the fraction of its mapped fragments at each length. It answers how long the surviving DNA fragments are.
    How to read: ancient DNA is fragmented, so a curve piled at short lengths fits it. A curve with a wide tail towards long fragments looks like a modern library, a possible contamination even when the damage curve passes. The two strands of a library should follow each other.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17715061/ and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22479540/
  kind: profile
  config:
    x_title: Fragment length (bp)
    y_title: Fraction of mapped fragments
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    series: series
    x: length
    y: fraction

- component: figure
  title: Fragment counts by length
  description: |-
    Each line is a library and strand: the number of mapped fragments at each length. It answers how many fragments, not only what share, fall at each length.
    How to read: a library with far more fragments dominates the plot, so use the profile tile to compare shapes. A sharp drop at the shortest lengths reflects the minimum length kept by the mapping step.
    Source: https://damageprofiler.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contents/output.html
  visu_type: line
  dict_kwargs:
    x: length
    y: occurrences
    color: series
    labels:
      length: Fragment length (bp)
      occurrences: Mapped fragments
      series: Library and strand

- component: card
  title: Mapped fragments
  description: |-
    The hero number is the count of mapped fragments over every library in view, and the bars split it by strand. It answers how many fragments the length distribution holds and whether the strands are balanced.
    How to read: the two strands should be of similar size. A strong imbalance points to a mapping or library issue.
  column: occurrences
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: strand
  top_n_count: 2
  caption: fragments, by strand

- component: card
  title: Fragments at the most common length
  description: |-
    The hero number is the largest count of fragments at a single length, and the histogram shows how counts are distributed over the length bins. It answers how peaked the length distribution is.
    How to read: a high maximum against a low median means the fragments cluster at a narrow range of lengths, as in a sheared or degraded library.
  column: occurrences
  aggregation: max
  aggregations:
  - median
  secondary_layout: histogram
  caption: distribution across length bins

- component: card
  title: Fragment length range
  description: |-
    The hero number is the longest fragment length present in the table, with the shortest beside it. It answers how wide the length window of the run is.
    How to read: the window reflects the lengths the mapping kept, not the lengths in the sample. Read the profile for the shape.
  column: length
  aggregation: max
  aggregations:
  - min
  secondary_layout: vertical
  caption: longest and shortest length

- component: table
  title: Fragment length table
  description: |-
    Each row is a length bin of one library and strand, with its fragment count and its fraction of the library. It answers the exact numbers behind the length curves.
    How to read: filter to one library and strand to read its distribution.
  page_size: 25

- component: advanced_viz
  id: eager_damage_profile
  title: Misincorporation profile
  description: |-
    Each line is a substitution type at one end of the reads: its frequency at each distance from the 5' or 3' end, with C to T and G to A highlighted by default and the other substitutions drawn muted. It answers whether the library carries the deamination damage of ancient DNA.
    How to read: ancient DNA shows C to T rising towards the 5' end and G to A towards the 3' end on a double-stranded library, while the other substitutions stay low and flat. Flat lines at both ends mean little damage. Check the fragment length profile before calling a library authentic.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17715061/ and https://damageprofiler.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contents/output.html
  kind: damage_profile
  roles:
    sample: sample
    end: end
    position: position
    base_change: base_change
    frequency: frequency

- component: figure
  title: Misincorporation frequency by position
  description: |-
    Each line is a substitution type at the 5' or 3' end of the reads, with its frequency at each distance from that end. It answers how damage decays away from the read ends.
    How to read: a high frequency at the first base that falls within a few positions is the shape of terminal deamination. A line that stays high along the read points to chemical damage or errors in the data and not to ancient DNA damage.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17715061/
  visu_type: line
  dict_kwargs:
    x: position
    y: frequency
    color: base_change
    line_dash: end
    labels:
      position: Distance from the read end (bases)
      frequency: Substitution frequency
      base_change: Substitution
      end: Read end

- component: card
  title: Strongest substitution
  description: |-
    The hero number is the highest substitution frequency in the table, and the bars rank the substitution types by their own maximum. It answers which substitution stands out and how strongly.
    How to read: C to T and G to A leading the ranking is the deamination pattern expected of ancient DNA. Another substitution on top is not explained by damage and deserves a look at the data.
    Source: https://damageprofiler.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contents/output.html
  column: frequency
  aggregation: max
  aggregations:
  - average
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: base_change
  top_n_count: 3
  caption: highest frequency, by substitution

- component: table
  title: Misincorporation table
  description: |-
    Each row is a substitution type at one position from one read end of a library, with its frequency. It answers the exact numbers behind the damage curves.
    How to read: filter to position 0 to compare the terminal frequency of each library.
